title: Clean hands, tidy depot: workplace hygiene from the toilet to the fridge body
prepared_by: Monaro Milk safety (weekly toolbox talk), on a topic requested by Mick Johnson
summary: Mick Johnson asked for a talk on workplace hygiene, from washing your hands after the toilet through to general tidiness. This week covers two things that go together: keeping ourselves clean so we do not spread illness, and keeping the depot, docks, yard, cabs and fridge bodies tidy so that dirt, spills, rubbish and pests do not reach people or the bottled milk we carry. Each point is labelled LAW (WHS law or the Food Standards Code), GUIDANCE (regulator advice) or GOOD PRACTICE. Our milk is sealed, so kitchen rules for open food (aprons, hairnets, tongs) are not the main message. Site details such as our amenities, our illness rule, our cleaning schedule and pest control are being confirmed by Mick or the GM. They are listed under Follow-up actions, not stated here as fact.
key_risk: Poor personal hygiene and an untidy workplace let illness, dirt, spills and pests reach people or the packaged milk we carry. Unwashed hands after the toilet, someone with gastro still handling crates, an uncovered cut, a leaking bottle left in a fridge body, rubbish on the dock or pests in a truck or store can contaminate crates and packaging, or the milk itself if a bottle is broken or open. The same mess causes slips and trips on wet, icy or cluttered floors at the dock, in the yard and inside fridge bodies. SafeWork NSW says slips, trips and falls on the same level are the most common cause of serious injuries at work in NSW after hazardous manual tasks.
drivers_need_to_know: Why this applies to us. The Food Standards Code says handling of food includes storing, transporting and delivering it (Standard 3.1.1). So anyone who handles crates of bottled milk or works in the fridge bodies is a food handler under Standard 3.2.2 (LAW). WHS law also requires a clean, safe workplace and proper facilities. Hygiene here is both a food-safety duty and a WHS duty.

Wash your hands after the toilet, every time. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 15(2)): a food handler must wash their hands immediately after using the toilet, and whenever their hands are likely to contaminate food. LAW (clause 15(4)): use the hand-washing facilities provided, clean thoroughly with soap (or another effective means) and warm running water, then dry thoroughly on a single-use towel or another way that will not put germs back on your hands. NSW Food Authority transport GUIDANCE also lists after meal breaks. GOOD PRACTICE: also wash after cleaning, handling rubbish or dealing with a leak, before you go back to crates or the fridge body.

How to wash properly (FSANZ GUIDANCE): wet your hands under warm running water, lather with soap, and scrub your fingers, palms, wrists, the backs of your hands and under your nails for at least 15 seconds. Rinse under warm running water and dry thoroughly with a single-use towel or a hand dryer. NSW Food Authority checklist: do not dry your hands on your clothes or reusable cloths.

On the road. GUIDANCE (SafeWork NSW approved code): workers away from base must have access to other toilets, for example public toilets or toilets at clients' premises, and should be told where they are. If there is no basin, the code says workers should have an alternative such as a water container with soap and paper towels, hand wipes or alcohol-based hand sanitiser. GOOD PRACTICE: use a basin with soap and water whenever one is there. Sanitiser or wipes are the fallback, not the first choice. If a toilet or basin you rely on is closed, dirty or has no soap, tell your supervisor.

If you are crook, especially with gastro. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 14): if you have diarrhoea, vomiting, a sore throat with fever, fever or jaundice, or you know you have or carry a foodborne illness, you must tell your supervisor and must not handle food where it is reasonably likely to be contaminated. You must also tell your supervisor if you think you may have contaminated food. LAW (clause 16): the business must keep you off that work. If you were excluded because you were known to have or carry a foodborne disease, you can only go back to food handling after a doctor advises you no longer have it or carry it. FSANZ GUIDANCE: return when a doctor says you are well enough, usually 48 hours after symptoms stop. Our own Monaro Milk rule on who to call and when you can come back is being confirmed (see Follow-up actions). Being sick can also make you unfit to drive (see the 9 November talk).

Your health information is private. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 18(2)): what you tell us about illness must not be shared without your consent, except with the proprietor or an authorised officer. It can only be used to manage the risk of food contamination.

Cuts, sores and discharges. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 15(1)(d)): any bandage or dressing on an exposed part of your body must be completely covered with a waterproof covering. NSW Food Authority GUIDANCE gives a glove as an example. LAW (clause 14(2)): the Standard calls an infected skin lesion or a discharge from the ear, nose or eye a 'condition'. If it could contaminate food, tell your supervisor and take all practicable measures to stop contamination.

Clothing and habits. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 15(1)): keep your outer clothing clean enough for the handling you are doing. Do not eat, sneeze, blow or cough over unprotected food or surfaces likely to touch food. Do not spit, smoke or use tobacco where food is handled. NSW Food Authority transport GUIDANCE: wear clean clothing at the start of each day, and do not smoke around food products at any time. The NSW Food Authority personal hygiene checklist adds no vaping in food handling areas. GOOD PRACTICE: no eating or drinking inside the fridge body, and keep personal gear out of the load space.

Clean fridge bodies, crates and pallets. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clauses 10, 19(2) and 21): when transporting food, protect it from the likelihood of contamination. Keep the parts of vehicles used to transport food free of any build-up of food waste, dirt, grease or other visible matter, and in good repair and working order. GOOD PRACTICE: before loading, check the floor, walls, door seals and drains of the fridge body for spilt milk, broken bottles, rubbish or pest signs. Keep dirty, broken or wet crates and damaged stock out of the load and report them. A clean, dry floor also helps stop pallets sliding (see the 2 November talk).

Leaks and broken bottles. GOOD PRACTICE: set the damaged bottle and any milk-soaked crates aside so they do not go out to a customer. Put on gloves, clean up the spill, take the gloves off and then wash your hands. Gloves do not replace hand washing. NSW Food Authority GUIDANCE: cleaning removes dirt and residue, while sanitising reduces harmful microorganisms. A surface that touches food needs both.

Tidy dock, yard and cab. GUIDANCE (SafeWork NSW approved code): clean up spills on floors straight away, keep walkways clear, store work materials neatly and remove waste regularly. SafeWork NSW lists spills, clutter, poor lighting, ice or water on cold room floors, rushing and the wrong footwear as common causes of slips and trips. GOOD PRACTICE: keep dock plates and doorways clear of shrink wrap, broken crates and pallets. Do not leave food scraps or rubbish in the cab, because they attract pests and become a trip hazard. Keeping the cab tidy is housekeeping, not an NHVR rule. Your NHVR daily check still needs clear windscreens, wipers and mirrors.

Pests. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 24): the business must take all practicable measures to keep pests out of food premises and to eradicate and prevent pest harbourage on the premises and in the parts of vehicles used to transport food. No live animals where food is handled. FSANZ GUIDANCE: do not transport food with pets or other animals. GOOD PRACTICE: report droppings, rodents, cockroaches, birds or flies in the depot, a cool room, a cab or a fridge body the same day. Keep doors shut when you can and keep bins lidded.

Temperature, in one line. LAW (Standard 3.2.2 clause 10): potentially hazardous food such as milk must be transported under temperature control, which for cold food means 5°C or below. That topic is for another week. This week is about cleanliness.
supervisors_must_check: Depot toilets and hand basins are clean, working, stocked with soap, warm water, toilet paper and single-use towels or a dryer, and have bins. Check them before early starts and after late finishes. LAW: WHS Regulation sections 40 to 41 (facilities must be adequate, clean, safe, accessible and in good working order, so far as is reasonably practicable). For food handlers, Standard 3.2.2 clause 17 and Standard 3.2.3 clause 16 also apply. What we actually have on site is being confirmed (Follow-up 1).
Clean drinking water is available free of charge and kept separate from toilets and washing facilities, and the meal area is hygienic (GUIDANCE: SafeWork NSW approved code).

Drivers know where they can use a toilet and wash their hands on their regular runs, and have a fallback for when there is no basin (GUIDANCE: approved code, mobile workers). Drivers are not made to feel rushed out of a toilet stop.

Every food handler has been told their health and hygiene obligations (LAW: Standard 3.2.2 clause 18(1)) and has food safety and hygiene skills and knowledge to match their work (LAW: clause 3). No one is pressured to work with gastro symptoms. Anyone with symptoms is kept off product handling where contamination is reasonably likely (LAW: clause 16). Illness information is kept confidential (LAW: clause 18(2)).

Fridge bodies, crates and the dock are free of any build-up of food waste, dirt, grease or other visible matter, and in good repair (LAW: Standard 3.2.2 clauses 19 and 21). Damaged or leaking stock is kept out of the load. Whether a documented cleaning schedule and cleaning-inspection records exist is being confirmed (Follow-up 4). NSW Food Authority says dairy food transporters must have both.

Pest signs are looked for and reported, and whatever pest-control arrangement is in place is actually followed and recorded. LAW: Standard 3.2.2 clause 24. GUIDANCE: NSW Food Authority recommends a licensed pest controller and records of inspections and treatments. The current arrangement is being confirmed (Follow-up 6).

Spill gear, bins, brooms and wet-floor controls are where they are needed, walkways and dock plates are clear, and ice or water in fridge bodies and on the dock is dealt with (GUIDANCE: SafeWork NSW slips, trips and falls; approved code, housekeeping).
Everyone who attends has signed on to this talk in the Monaro Milk TB Talk app.
discussion_questions: After a toilet stop on the road, where do you actually wash your hands, and what do you do if there is no soap or the basin is out of order?
If you woke up with vomiting or diarrhoea before an early start, who would you call, and what might push you to come in anyway?
Where on our dock, in the yard or inside a fridge body is it currently wet, messy or cluttered enough to cause a slip, attract pests or dirty the crates?
What do you do when a bottle leaks in the body or a crate turns up dirty or broken, and who needs to know?
What would make it easier to keep the amenities, the dock and the trucks clean on early starts and late finishes?
practical_checklist: Washed hands with soap and warm running water after the toilet and dried them on a single-use towel or dryer
Washed hands after meal breaks, cleaning, handling rubbish or a leak, before going back to crates or the fridge body
On the road: used a known toilet and basin, or the fallback if no basin was available. Reported any unusable facility
Unwell with vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, sore throat with fever or jaundice: told the supervisor and stayed off product handling
Any dressing on exposed skin covered with a waterproof covering
Clean clothing at the start of the day. No smoking or vaping around product. No eating or drinking in the fridge body
Fridge body checked before loading: floor, walls, door seals and drains clean, with no spilt milk, broken bottles, rubbish or pest signs
Dirty, broken or wet crates and damaged or leaking stock kept out of the load and reported
Spills at the dock, in the yard or in the body cleaned up straight away. Walkways and dock plates clear
Rubbish in bins, not on the floor. Cab free of food scraps and litter
Suitable footwear for wet or icy floors. Gloves for spills and broken bottles, then hands washed
Pest sightings, leaks and amenity problems reported the same day
required_records: Toolbox talk sign-on for this talk in the Monaro Milk TB Talk app (CSV export or printed register).
Illness and unfit-for-work reports: who was stood down, when they returned and, where Standard 3.2.2 clause 16(3) applies, the doctor's advice. Keep these confidential (clause 18(2)).
Amenities checks and restocking or repair records for toilets, hand basins, drinking water and the meal area.

Cleaning records for fridge bodies, crates, docks and other transport equipment, including any documented cleaning schedule and cleaning-inspection and corrective-action records (NSW Food Authority expects these of dairy food transporters).
Pest inspection and treatment records, and any corrective action.
Hazard and incident reports for spills, leaking or damaged product, slips and trips, and what was done about each.
Records showing food handlers were told their health and hygiene obligations (Standard 3.2.2 clause 18(1)) and have the skills and knowledge for their work (clause 3).

follow_up_actions.action: Confirm what amenities we have at the depot and check them: number and type of toilets, hand basins with warm water, soap, single-use towels or a dryer, bins, sanitary disposal, drinking water and the meal area. Restock or repair anything not working, including before early starts.

Confirm or write down Monaro Milk's illness and gastro rule: who to call, including before an early start; when someone stays off product handling or off driving; what is needed before they return (including doctor's advice where Standard 3.2.2 clause 16(3) applies); and whether we use FSANZ's 'usually 48 hours after symptoms stop' guidance. Tell all staff.

List where drivers can use a toilet and wash their hands on regular runs (customer sites and public facilities), and decide on a fallback for each truck when no basin is available (water and soap with paper towels, wipes or sanitiser).

Confirm whether a documented cleaning schedule exists for fridge bodies, docks, crates and transport equipment, with cleaning-inspection and corrective-action records. If it does, check it is followed. If not, draft one.
Walk the dock, yard and a sample of fridge bodies looking at housekeeping, spills, damaged crates, ice or water, and pest signs. Fix what can be fixed on the spot and record the rest.
Confirm the current pest-control arrangement (licensed contractor or in-house plan), that inspections happen, and that records are kept.

Confirm our NSW Food Authority licence position for wholesale transport of processed dairy (and which vehicles are listed). Confirm whether food safety and hygiene skills and knowledge are covered at induction.
Follow up any amenities, illness, spill, pest or housekeeping issue raised at this talk.

sources_reviewed.name: FSANZ / Federal Register of Legislation
sources_reviewed.title: Food Standards Code, Standard 3.2.2 Food Safety Practices and General Requirements (Australia only), Authorised Version F2025C00834
sources_reviewed.note: Read the latest compilation (13 Aug 2025). Used: definitions (symptom, condition, temperature control), cl 3 skills and knowledge, cl 10 transport, cl 14 to 18 health and hygiene (handwashing times and method, illness reporting and exclusion, medical advice before return, confidentiality), cl 19 and 21 vehicle cleanliness and repair, cl 24 pests.

sources_reviewed.name: FSANZ / Federal Register of Legislation
sources_reviewed.title: Food Standards Code, Standard 3.1.1 Interpretation and Application, Authorised Version F2025C00604
sources_reviewed.note: Definition: handling of food includes storing, transporting and delivering. Food handler definition. Food premises excludes vehicles used only to transport food.

sources_reviewed.name: FSANZ / Federal Register of Legislation
sources_reviewed.title: Food Standards Code, Standard 3.2.3 Food Premises and Equipment, Authorised Version F2021C00674
sources_reviewed.note: Latest compilation. Cl 3: premises designed so they can be cleaned and keep pests out. Cl 16: adequate toilets for food handlers. Cl 17: food transport vehicles must protect food and be able to be effectively cleaned.

sources_reviewed.name: SafeWork NSW
sources_reviewed.title: Code of Practice: Managing the work environment and facilities (NSW approved code)
sources_reviewed.note: Approved under WHS Act s274. Used: facilities duty (clean, safe, accessible, good working order), housekeeping, drinking water, toilets and hand washing, mobile workers' access to public or client toilets, and hand-hygiene alternatives where there is no basin.

sources_reviewed.name: SafeWork NSW
sources_reviewed.title: WHS codes of practice
sources_reviewed.note: Confirms the current NSW approved facilities code is the August 2019 version.

sources_reviewed.name: SafeWork NSW
sources_reviewed.title: Slips, trips and falls on the same level
sources_reviewed.note: Slips, trips and falls are the most common cause of serious injuries at work in NSW after hazardous manual tasks. Causes include spills, clutter, lighting, ice or water on cold room floors, rushing and footwear. Points to WHS Regulation 2025 sections 40 to 41.

sources_reviewed.name: SafeWork NSW
sources_reviewed.title: Facilities at work
sources_reviewed.note: Must provide clean, safe and accessible toilets, drinking water, washing and eating facilities. A tidy workplace reduces slips and trips.

sources_reviewed.name: Safe Work Australia
sources_reviewed.title: Model Code of Practice: Managing the work environment and facilities (landing page)
sources_reviewed.note: Context only: the national model was last updated 19 Dec 2025. Safe Work Australia says to check with your regulator whether it has legal effect. In NSW we rely on the 2019 approved code.

sources_reviewed.name: FSANZ
sources_reviewed.title: Health and hygiene: advice for food handlers
sources_reviewed.note: Guidance: the 15-second handwash method, when to wash hands, and returning when a doctor says you are well (usually 48 hours after symptoms stop). Labelled as guidance.

sources_reviewed.name: FSANZ
sources_reviewed.title: Transporting food safely
sources_reviewed.note: Use clean vehicles, check packaging is secure, do not transport food with pets or other animals, keep cold food at 5°C or colder.

sources_reviewed.name: NSW Food Authority
sources_reviewed.title: Food transport vehicles
sources_reviewed.note: Wholesale transport of milk or dairy products needs a Food Authority licence. Transporter hygiene: clean clothing each day, no handling food when ill, waterproof covering on wounds, wash hands after the toilet and meal breaks, no smoking around food. Skills and knowledge needed.

sources_reviewed.name: NSW Food Authority
sources_reviewed.title: Dairy food transport vehicles
sources_reviewed.note: Dairy food transporters must have a documented cleaning schedule, with routine cleaning inspections and corrective-action records. Vehicles must be able to be cleaned. Used to frame follow-ups, not as a claim about our site.

sources_reviewed.name: NSW Food Authority
sources_reviewed.title: Food handler personal hygiene checklist (FA797-2609)
sources_reviewed.note: Waterproof covering on cuts (for example a glove), clean clothes, no vaping or smoking in food handling areas, do not dry hands on clothes. Kitchen-only items (aprons, hairnets) not used as rules.

sources_reviewed.name: NSW Food Authority
sources_reviewed.title: Pest control in food businesses (FA627-2609)
sources_reviewed.note: Take all practicable measures against pests. Use a licensed pest controller. Keep doors closed, use sealed bins, inspect regularly and keep records.

sources_reviewed.name: NSW Food Authority
sources_reviewed.title: Cleaning and sanitising (FA450-2608)
sources_reviewed.note: Cleaning removes dirt and grease. Sanitising reduces harmful microorganisms. Anything that touches food needs both.

sources_reviewed.name: NHVR
sources_reviewed.title: Creating heavy vehicle daily checks (fact sheet)
sources_reviewed.note: Checked for any cab hygiene rule and found none. The daily check covers mirrors, windscreens, wipers and washers for clear vision.
